differential: Meniere's Disease
The combination of hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness points towards Meniere's disease, although further information is needed to confirm episodic nature.
Acoustic Neuroma
Unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and dizziness can be indicative of an acoustic neuroma, a benign tumor affecting the vestibulocochlear nerve.
Labyrinthitis
Inflammation of the inner ear can cause hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo.
Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
Although primarily causing vertigo, BPPV can sometimes be associated with imbalance and atypical presentations involving tinnitus or hearing changes.
Otosclerosis
While typically presenting with conductive hearing loss, otosclerosis can sometimes cause sensorineural components and tinnitus, potentially leading to dizziness.
eliminated: Unlikely given the chronicity and presence of dizziness and tinnitus.

differential: Neurofibromatosis Type 2
The presence of sensorineural hearing loss, facial muscle weakness, and unsteady gait suggests a possible tumor affecting cranial nerves, which is characteristic of NF2.
Sarcoidosis
The combination of sensorineural hearing loss, facial nerve palsy, and skin lesions (plaques/papules) could indicate neurosarcoidosis.
Lyme disease
Bilateral facial nerve palsy, hearing loss, and skin manifestations can occur in Lyme disease.
Cholesterol Embolism
The presence of skin plaques/papules along with neurological symptoms could be related to cholesterol emboli affecting the brain and inner ear.
Fabry disease
This lysosomal storage disorder can present with skin lesions (angiokeratomas), hearing loss, and neurological symptoms.
eliminated: No diagnoses have been definitively ruled out yet.

differential: Acoustic Neuroma
Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, dizziness, and facial weakness are classic symptoms.
Multiple Sclerosis
Dizziness, sensorineural hearing loss, facial weakness, and unsteady gait can be associated with MS plaques in the brainstem.
Ramsay Hunt Syndrome
Facial weakness and sensorineural hearing loss, along with dizziness, could be caused by varicella-zoster virus reactivation affecting the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves.
Lyme Disease
Bilateral facial nerve palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, dizziness, and unsteady gait can occur in disseminated Lyme disease.

Although less likely in a 23-year-old, a brainstem glioma could explain the cranial nerve deficits and gait instability.
eliminated: Physical exam was unremarkable except for neurological findings, making simple obstruction unlikely.

differential: Bilateral Vestibular Schwannomas

The presence of bilateral masses at the cerebellopontine angle in a young adult with hearing loss, dizziness, and facial weakness is highly suggestive of this condition, especially given the association with NF2.
Meningioma

Meningiomas can occur in the cerebellopontine angle and internal auditory meatus, presenting with similar symptoms of hearing loss, dizziness, and facial weakness due to compression of cranial nerves.
Epidermoid Cyst
Epidermoid cysts in the cerebellopontine angle can cause similar symptoms to vestibular schwannomas due to their location and slow growth, compressing nearby structures.
Arachnoid Cyst
Although less common, arachnoid cysts in the cerebellopontine angle can present with hearing loss, dizziness, and facial weakness due to mass effect on the surrounding cranial nerves and brainstem.
Neurofibroma
While vestibular schwannomas are the most common neurofibromas in this location, other neurofibromas can occur in the cerebellopontine angle and internal auditory meatus, causing similar symptoms.
eliminated: The MRI findings of masses in the cerebellopontine angle and internal auditory meatus make Meniere's disease less likely.
